options.metric: Annual number of motorists killed in police-reported crashes, summed from number_of_motorist_killed.
options.denominator: None; this is a count, not an exposure-adjusted rate.
options.reason: A careful analyst may use annual death counts to show the recorded fatality burden even though they do not measure risk per mile.
options.answer: Recorded motorist deaths fell from 110 in 2013 to 81 in 2025 (about 26% fewer), but these counts do not establish a decline in risk per mile.
options.interpretation: For each calendar year from 2013 through 2025, this chart sums the number_of_motorist_killed values across all police-reported NYC crashes dated in that year, so the recorded count falls from 110 in 2013 to 81 in 2025. This is a defensible view of annual fatality burden, but it has no denominator and therefore cannot establish whether a motorist's risk per mile declined; the file contains no miles-driven exposure. The check found 2,132,218 dated crashes in these years, zero null crash dates, and zero missing motorist-death values, so no selected rows were dropped or treated differently; every year, including 2025's 85,546 crashes, has recorded dates from Jan 1 through Dec 31, and no tested placeholder dates occurred. All rows were kept; the full date endpoints do not verify reporting completeness.

options.metric: Motorists killed per 1,000 police-reported crashes in each calendar year.
options.denominator: Number of police-reported crashes with a usable motorist-death count in that calendar year; multiply deaths per crash by 1,000.
options.chart_type: Line chart of annual deaths per 1,000 crashes.
options.reason: A careful analyst may choose a crash-normalized fatality rate as a closer available proxy for risk than raw counts, while recognizing that crashes are not miles driven.
options.answer: Motorist deaths per 1,000 reported crashes rose from 0.54 in 2013 to 0.95 in 2025 (about 75%), so this crash-based measure did not decline, although it is not risk per mile.
options.interpretation: For each calendar year from 2013 through 2025, the chart divides the sum of number_of_motorist_killed by the number of police-reported NYC crashes with that field present, then multiplies by 1,000; the value rises from 0.54 per 1,000 crashes in 2013 to 0.95 in 2025. This is a defensible crash-normalized fatality measure and is more normalized than a count, but it cannot establish whether a motorist's risk per mile declined because the dataset has no miles-driven exposure and crashes are not a measure of driving distance. The check found 2,132,218 dated crashes, zero null crash dates, and zero missing motorist-death values, so no rows were excluded from either numerator population or denominator; dates span Jan 1 to Dec 31 in every year, including 2025's 85,546 crashes, and no tested placeholder dates occurred. All eligible rows were kept, while the full date endpoints do not verify reporting completeness.
